title: The Ethics of Designed Attention
passage:
Institutions often behave as though categories merely describe reality, but categories can also shape what an institution notices. Once a classification becomes routine, observations that do not fit it may be treated as exceptions rather than as evidence that the classification itself is incomplete.

This creates a subtle problem. An institution can become more efficient at processing familiar cases while simultaneously becoming less sensitive to unfamiliar ones. Correcting the problem requires more than adding another category. It may require examining the assumptions that determined which distinctions were considered important in the first place.

The argument is not that categories are useless. On the contrary, categories make coordination possible. The difficulty arises when a useful tool is mistaken for a complete description and the unclassified remainder disappears from view.

The title, then, points to a question of method rather than a single answer. The most reliable approach is to distinguish observation from interpretation and to state the limits of the evidence alongside the conclusion.
